Design leaves tracks.

Like a gecko adapting to its surroundings, design changes across time while carrying traces of its origins. Follow the visual tracks of earlier movements into the graphics and interfaces of today.

BEGIN YOUR INVESTIGATION

Three ways to explore

01 / TRACE

Find the ancestors

Start with a contemporary design profile and reveal the historical traits that it shares.

02 / EXAMINE

Study the movements

Explore original interpretive specimens, dates, principles, and historical references.

03 / EXPERIMENT

Build visual DNA

Combine lettering, composition, and palette choices in a live typographic poster.

THE MOVEMENT ARCHIVE / RECORDS

Visual evolution, catalogued.

Explore 21 design movements and approaches. Open a record for historical context, key examples, recognisable visual characteristics, legacy, comparative analysis, and cautions about oversimplifying the history. Specimens are newly created illustrations, not historical artifacts.

CURATORIAL NOTE / HOW TO READ THE ARCHIVE

Design is a network, not a straight line.

These records describe movements, schools, and recurring visual approaches. Their illustrated specimens are new interpretations—not reproductions of historic artworks. Explore each record for distinguishing traits, historical context, and source links; an influence is not necessarily a direct lineage.

01 / FORM

Identify a visual trait

Begin with observable evidence: line, shape, layout, type, materials, or color. Name what you actually see before assigning a historical movement.

02 / CONTEXT

Locate its circumstances

Dates, geography, technologies, institutions, audiences, and media help explain why a style emerged. Similar looks can arise for different reasons.

03 / CONNECTION

Test an influence claim

A shared feature is not proof of direct inheritance. Seek documented contact, publications, education, or statements when describing influence.

04 / SOURCE

Check the evidence

Use museum collections and primary documents. The specimen images in this atlas are new teaching illustrations, not historic originals.

FIELD GLOSSARY / RESEARCH TOOLS

Read the visual language

Useful terms for comparing designs across time.

Hierarchy
The relative prominence of elements that establishes reading order.
Grid
An alignment framework that organizes spacing and proportion.
Photomontage
Composition built by assembling photographic fragments.
Asymmetry
Balance achieved without mirroring the two sides.
Negative space
Empty areas that shape how elements are perceived.
Ornament
Decorative form that may carry symbolic, cultural, or structural meaning.
Visual citation
A traceable reference supporting a claim or interpretation about design.
Specimen
A study image showing visual traits; here it is interpretive rather than an original artifact.
GECKOPEDIA / RESEARCH HANDBOOK

Reading the evidence behind a visual style

Use these questions when examining an artwork, advertisement, product, interface, or movement. Historical facts and your own visual interpretation should remain clearly separated.

01 / DATE & PLACE

When did it take shape?

Identify the earliest known examples, the period of wider recognition, and the geographical context. A movement's date range is approximate; techniques often persist much longer than its original institutional group.

02 / MEDIA

Where did it circulate?

Look beyond posters. Ideas pass through books, exhibitions, architecture, textiles, photography, schools, catalogs, consumer products and contemporary interfaces. The medium shapes what a design can communicate.

03 / FORM

What can you actually see?

Record typography, grid, image treatment, spacing, scale, color relationships, line quality and ornament before assigning a label. Compare specific visible features rather than relying on a general resemblance.

04 / MAKING

How was it produced?

Printing methods, available materials, photography, mass production and software affect visual outcomes. The same form can mean something different when handmade, mechanically reproduced or generated digitally.

05 / AUDIENCE

Who was it for?

Ask what the designer, publisher or institution wanted the work to do. A political poster, an exhibition catalog, commercial packaging and a software dashboard have different needs and constraints.

06 / EVIDENCE

Is this a proven influence?

Formal similarities are useful clues, not proof. Stronger connections involve correspondence, shared education, citations, exhibitions, published manifestos, archives or statements from the people involved.

Method: start from an object and a question, consult the linked museum or institutional references in its record, and distinguish description, documented history, and your own hypothesis.

RESEARCH NOTES / BIBLIOGRAPHY

Sources & methodology.

The archive privileges museums, national collections, and established design-history resources. Relationship labels identify whether a link is supported by a source or is an interpretive visual comparison.

AN IMPORTANT DISTINCTION

A shared visual characteristic is not proof of direct influence. “Documented” relationships are tied to historical reference material; “interpretive” links identify formal similarities that could be useful for study. The original visual specimens in this app demonstrate general traits and are not authentic archival reproductions.
